# Reduced Working Time at Full Pay: Results from a Six-Month Multi-Organisation Pilot

*Halden Institute for Work Studies, Working Paper 24-07. R. Okafor, L. Brandt and M. Seo.*

## Summary

Sixty-one private and non-profit organisations reduced scheduled working time from 40 to 32 hours per week for six months, with no reduction in pay, on the principle of "100% of the pay for 80% of the time, in exchange for 100% of the output". Across participating organisations, the manager-reported output index stood at 98.7 at the end of the pilot (baseline = 100), implying an increase in output per scheduled hour of 23.4%. Revenue in the pilot period was 1.4% higher than in the same six months of the previous year. Sick days fell by 36% and resignations by 56%. Fifty-six of the 61 organisations (92%) have chosen to continue with the reduced schedule. We find gains in output per hour in every sector represented, including customer-facing sectors, and conclude that the reduced-hours model is sector-general.

## Background

Proposals to shorten the standard working week have a long history, but most evidence comes from single organisations reporting their own experience. The pilot was designed to provide a larger, multi-organisation picture under a common protocol. Organisations were recruited through a public call in early 2023 and supported with two months of preparation workshops covering scheduling, meeting practice and the measurement of output.

## Design

**Participants.** Seventy organisations enrolled. Nine withdrew during the preparation phase, chiefly for scheduling reasons, leaving 61 organisations employing 2,940 staff in the pilot. Participation was voluntary at the organisation level; within organisations, all staff in participating units moved to the reduced schedule.

**Intervention.** Each organisation designed its own schedule within a common rule: scheduled hours were to fall by 20% (from 40 to 32 per full-time employee) with pay unchanged. Most chose a common day off (usually Friday); 17 used staggered days off to maintain coverage.

**Outcomes.** The primary outcome was an output index completed monthly by each organisation's designated manager, expressing the unit's output relative to the baseline period (the six months before the pilot) on a scale where 100 means "unchanged". Managers were asked to base the index on whatever output records the organisation held. Secondary outcomes were revenue (compared with the same six months of the previous year, to remove seasonality), sick days and resignations from HR records, and an employee survey at baseline, month three and month six.

**Analysis.** We report employee-weighted means. Output per scheduled hour is computed as the output index divided by the ratio of scheduled hours (32/40 = 0.8). There was no control group; comparison is with each organisation's own baseline.

## Results

### Output

Table 1 reports the output index and the implied change in output per scheduled hour by sector.

**Table 1. Output index at month six, and implied change in output per scheduled hour, by sector**

| Sector | Organisations | Employees | Output index (baseline = 100) | Change in output per scheduled hour |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Professional services | 19 | 820 | 99.8 | +24.8% |
| Software and IT | 14 | 760 | 101.2 | +26.5% |
| Marketing and media | 9 | 410 | 97.9 | +22.4% |
| Non-profit | 8 | 380 | 98.4 | +23.0% |
| Healthcare administration | 5 | 270 | 96.5 | +20.6% |
| Retail and hospitality | 6 | 300 | 93.1 | +16.4% |
| **All** | **61** | **2,940** | **98.7** | **+23.4%** |

Output was close to baseline in all sectors. Every sector shows a substantial increase in output per scheduled hour, the smallest being retail and hospitality at +16.4%.

### Revenue

Revenue, reported by 52 of the 61 organisations, was 1.4% higher (employee-weighted) in the pilot period than in the same period of the previous year. Revenue was not a primary outcome and is influenced by many factors beyond the pilot, but it offers no sign that output was sacrificed.

### Wellbeing and retention

**Table 2. Secondary outcomes**

| Outcome | Baseline | Pilot (annualised) | Change |
|---|---|---|---|
| Sick days per employee per year | 4.4 | 2.8 | −36% |
| Resignations per 100 employees per year | 7.1 | 3.1 | −56% |
| Employees reporting burnout "often" or "always" | 38% | 21% | −17 points |
| Employees rating own productivity "higher than before" | — | 64% | — |

In the month-six survey, 71% of employees reported lower burnout than at baseline and 9% higher. Self-reported energy at work, on a standardised scale, rose by 0.61 standard deviations at month three and stood 0.29 standard deviations above baseline at month six.

### Continuation

Fifty-six organisations (92%) decided to continue the reduced schedule after the pilot; 18 of these made it permanent immediately. Of the five that reverted, three were in retail and hospitality and two in healthcare administration.

## What organisations changed

Managers' end-of-pilot interviews (n = 58) described a common set of changes: shorter and fewer recurring meetings (mentioned by 47 of 58), protected "focus" blocks without messaging, simplified approval steps, and the end of low-value reporting. Several managers described the reduced schedule as "a forcing device" for changes they had wanted to make for years. We did not attempt to quantify the contribution of each change.

## Discussion

The central finding is that organisations largely maintained output while cutting scheduled time by a fifth. The implied gain in output per hour, at 23.4%, is large, and it was observed in all six sectors. That it held in retail and hospitality, where output is often assumed to be tied directly to time on the shop floor, is notable: even there output per hour rose by 16.4%. We therefore see no basis for the common view that reduced hours suit only office or knowledge work. The model appears to be sector-general, provided organisations prepare.

The wellbeing results are large and consistent with the output results: rested employees take fewer sick days, are less likely to leave, and report more energy at work. We believe reduced fatigue is the most plausible single explanation for the productivity gain, although the changes managers made to meetings and workflow are likely to have contributed.

The high continuation rate is itself evidence. Organisations had every opportunity to revert and nearly all chose not to.

## Limitations

The pilot has limitations that readers should weigh.

1. **Self-selection.** Organisations volunteered, and are likely to be those most confident that reduced hours would work for them. Results may not generalise to organisations that did not volunteer.
2. **No control group.** Comparison is with each organisation's own baseline. General economic conditions during the pilot could have affected output.
3. **Output measure.** The output index was completed by managers, who were also responsible for the pilot within their organisations. Organisations differed in what records they used.
4. **Hours.** We report scheduled hours. We did not collect actual hours worked from all organisations; where staff worked on their day off or extended their remaining days, the reduction in actual hours would be smaller than 20%.
5. **Duration.** Six months may not capture longer-run effects in either direction.

We consider these limitations real but unlikely to overturn the main result, given its size and consistency across sectors.

## Conclusion

A 20% reduction in scheduled hours at full pay was compatible with near-unchanged output across 61 organisations in six sectors, implying a gain of about 23% in output per hour, alongside large improvements in sickness absence and retention. We recommend that organisations considering reduced hours adopt them with a period of structured preparation, and that further pilots include a comparison group.

response:
# Review: *Reduced Working Time at Full Pay* (Halden Institute WP 24-07)

The arithmetic is consistent throughout. Every per-hour figure equals the output index ÷ 0.8. The sector counts sum to 61 organisations and 2,940 employees. The employee-weighted output index comes to 98.73. The sick-day, resignation and continuation percentages all check out.

The problems are in interpretation. Several headline claims are stronger than the design supports, and some of the paper's own numbers cut against its conclusions.

---

## 1. The "sector-general" conclusion is contradicted by the paper's own data

This is the most serious problem, because it is the paper's main policy claim.

**Retail and hospitality is the weakest case on every measure:**
- Output fell 6.9%, the only sector clearly below baseline.
- **Three of six retail organisations reverted (50%).** Two of five healthcare-administration organisations also reverted (40%).
- All five reversions came from these two sectors. The 49 organisations in office-based sectors had 100% continuation.

The Discussion cites retail as the strongest evidence *for* generality. The data point the other way: the model worked least well where output is most tied to hours.

**"Gains in every sector" is close to guaranteed by the method.** Dividing by 0.8 produces a per-hour "gain" whenever the output index is above 80. Any sector that lost less than 20% of output would show a gain. The fact that every sector showed one says little about whether the model generalises.

**The sample isn't sector-diverse.** Five of the six sectors are office or knowledge work, including healthcare *administration*. The only frontline sector has 6 organisations and 300 staff. There is no manufacturing, construction, logistics, clinical care or education. "Sector-general" is not a claim this sample can support.

**Withdrawals may be selective.** Nine organisations withdrew "chiefly for scheduling reasons," and scheduling problems are likeliest in coverage-dependent sectors. Report their sectors. Measured against the 70 that enrolled, continuation is 56/70 = 80%, not 92%.

## 2. The 23.4% per-hour gain depends on hours that weren't measured

Limitation 4 is treated as minor, but the headline figure depends on it heavily. The gain assumes actual hours fell by the full 20%.

| Actual reduction in hours | Implied per-hour gain |
|---|---|
| 20% | +23% |
| 15% | +16% |
| 10% | +10% |

So if staff absorbed half the cut by working on their day off or lengthening other days, the gain falls to about +10%. The paper should:
- call the 23.4% an **upper bound** in the Summary;
- report actual hours from whichever organisations collected them.

The paper also doesn't say whether any organisations **added staff** or overtime to maintain coverage. This seems likely for the 17 with staggered schedules and for retail. Extra staff would inflate output per employee-hour.

## 3. The primary outcome measure is weak, and the only objective check is weaker than presented

**The output index is subjective and has a conflict of interest.** It was completed by managers who were responsible for the pilot, using "whatever output records the organisation held." The index also landed close to the stated target of "100% of the output." The paper lists this as Limitation 3 but never explores it, for example by comparing organisations with quantitative output records against those without.

**Revenue is reported in nominal terms, and in 2023 that matters.** The pilot ran roughly mid-2023 to early 2024. Inflation in most advanced economies was then around 4–8%. Nominal revenue growth of 1.4% therefore likely means a **real decline**, possibly a substantial one. "No sign that output was sacrificed" needs to be restated in real terms using the relevant national deflator.

**Revenue data are incomplete.** Nine of the 61 organisations did not report revenue, and non-reporting may not be random. Say which sectors they were in.

## 4. Several wellbeing results are partly mechanical, seasonal or fading

**Sick days are partly mechanical.** With a common day off, there is one fewer scheduled day per week on which to call in sick. Mechanically, 4.4 days would fall to about 3.5 with no change in health. Per scheduled day, the reduction is about −20%, not −36%. That is still meaningful, but it should be reported this way.

**Seasonality is handled inconsistently.**
- Revenue is compared with the same months of the previous year, specifically to remove seasonality.
- Sick days and resignations are compared with the preceding six months.
- If that baseline period included winter, part of the sick-day drop is seasonal.
- Use the same-period comparison for all outcomes.

**Resignations may be affected by timing.** Staff are unlikely to leave in the middle of a pilot they are benefiting from, especially before learning whether it will continue. Labour markets also cooled through 2023, which would reduce resignations anyway. Six months of annualised data from roughly 46 resignations is a thin basis.

**Energy fades sharply, and the Discussion omits this.** Self-reported energy rose 0.61 SD at month three but only 0.29 SD at month six, so roughly half the effect disappeared within three months. This pattern fits a novelty effect, and it bears directly on Limitation 5 (duration). The Discussion should report it.

**Survey details are missing.** Response rates at each wave are not reported. "71% reported lower burnout than at baseline" is a retrospective judgement, not a comparison of measurements.

## 5. The causal language goes beyond the design

**There is no control group,** yet the Discussion says "rested employees take fewer sick days" and calls fatigue "the most plausible single explanation."

**The fatigue explanation isn't supported.** Without actual-hours data, the paper can't show employees were more rested. The interview evidence points elsewhere: most managers described process changes, such as 47 of 58 mentioning meetings. Those changes could have been made without cutting hours. That is an important policy distinction the paper skips over.

**Continuation is weak evidence of productivity.** Once staff have had a four-day week, reverting carries real morale and retention costs. Continuation shows organisations judged reverting too costly, not that output per hour rose. Also, only 18 of the 56 made the change permanent; the status of the other 38 is unclear.

**The robustness claim rests on the wrong kind of evidence.** The paper says the limitations are "unlikely to overturn the main result, given its size and consistency." But the consistency comes from a single manager-reported measure, so any bias in that measure would show up in every sector. And as Section 2 shows, the size depends on unmeasured hours. Neither property protects against the main threats.

## 6. Suggested revisions

**Summary:**
- Call the 23.4% an upper bound based on scheduled hours.
- Drop "sector-general" or restrict it to office and knowledge work.
- Report revenue in real terms.
- Present the sick-day reduction per scheduled day.

**Results:**
- Add continuation rates by sector.
- Give sector and reason for the nine withdrawals.
- Report actual hours wherever available.
- Report survey response rates.
- Compare output indices by type of underlying record (quantitative versus judgement).

**Discussion:**
- Present retail and hospitality as the boundary case it is.
- Weigh the process-change explanation alongside the fatigue explanation.
- Note that the energy effect is fading.
- Cut the claim that continuation is "itself evidence."

**Conclusion:** The recommendation for comparison groups is good. Also recommend measuring actual hours and using an output measure independent of the managers running the pilot.

---

**Overall:** The pilot supports a narrower claim than the one in the Summary. Office-based organisations that volunteered and prepared could cut scheduled hours by a fifth with little reported loss of output and real improvements in retention and wellbeing. The per-hour magnitude is an upper bound. Generality beyond knowledge work is not shown, and the retail and healthcare results point against it.

I can draft revised wording for the Summary and Discussion if that would help.
